entries.1:1: Babylon's king attacked Jerusalem and surrounded it. It shows that God's people could be defeated by a powerful enemy, yet God was still in control of what happened.
entries.1:2: God allowed the enemy king to capture Judah's king and take sacred objects from the temple to a pagan temple. Even in loss, the text says the Lord gave this into his hands, so God was not taken by surprise.
entries.1:3: The Babylonian king ordered his official to bring some young Israelites from royal or important families into his service. This was a way of taking the best of a conquered people and using them for the empire.
entries.1:4: These young men had to be healthy, handsome, and smart, and they were to be taught Babylonian language and learning. The king wanted them fully shaped by his culture so they could serve him well.
entries.1:5: The king provided them daily food and wine from his own table and planned three years of training. This was generous care, but it also tied their future to the king's favor.
entries.1:6: Four young men from Judah are named among those chosen. The story now focuses on real people facing pressure to fit into a foreign world.
entries.1:7: The official gave the four Israelites new Babylonian names. This was likely meant to reshape their identity, yet the text still remembers their original names.
entries.1:8: Daniel decided not to eat the king's food or wine because it would make him ritually unclean. He respectfully asked for permission rather than rebelling loudly, showing conviction with courtesy.
entries.1:9: God caused the official to look kindly on Daniel and feel sympathy for him. Daniel's courage did not stand alone; God was quietly working in the heart of the man in charge.
entries.1:10: The official was afraid the king would blame him if the young men looked worse than the others. He was willing to help but feared the consequences, which shows the real pressure Daniel's request created.
entries.1:11: Daniel turned to the guard directly responsible for their care. He kept working through the proper channels instead of giving up when the first answer was cautious.
entries.1:12: Daniel proposed a simple ten-day test of grain and water. He asked for a short trial rather than demanding a permanent change, which was a wise and humble approach.
entries.1:13: Daniel invited the guard to compare their appearance with the others and then decide. He trusted the outcome to speak for itself instead of insisting on his own way.
entries.1:14: The guard agreed to the ten-day test. Daniel's respectful request made room for someone in authority to say yes.
entries.1:15: After ten days, the four looked healthier than those eating the king's food. God honored Daniel's stand, though the text presents this as a specific outcome, not a promise that every diet choice brings visible reward.
entries.1:16: The guard then kept giving them grain instead of the king's meat and wine. The test led to a lasting change in their care.
entries.1:17: God gave these four young men unusual ability to learn and understand, and Daniel could interpret visions and dreams. Their gifts came from God, not just from their own effort or Babylonian training.
entries.1:18: When the training period ended, the official brought them before the king. The moment had come for their preparation to be tested in real service.
entries.1:19: The king spoke with them and found none equal to these four, so they entered his service. Their faithfulness and God's gifts placed them in a position of influence.
entries.1:20: Whenever the king tested them on matters of wisdom, they proved far better than all his magicians and advisers. God's wisdom stood out clearly against the best the empire could offer.
entries.1:21: Daniel remained in service until the first year of King Cyrus, a later Persian king. This note shows that Daniel's story stretched across decades and through major changes of power.
entries.2:1: A powerful king was so disturbed by his dreams that he could not sleep. Even someone with great power can be left frightened and restless by what he cannot understand.
entries.2:2: The king called in all his experts in magic and secret knowledge to tell him what his dream meant. People often look to all the wrong places for answers when they are afraid.
entries.2:3: The king told them he had a dream and was deeply troubled until he knew what it meant. Not knowing what something important means can weigh heavily on a person.
entries.2:4: The experts politely asked the king to tell them the dream so they could explain it. They were willing to help, but only if they had something to work with.
entries.2:5: The king threatened to have them cut to pieces and their homes destroyed if they failed. He was using fear and cruelty to force an answer out of them.
entries.2:6: He promised rich rewards and great honor if they succeeded. He was offering a strong incentive, but the threat still hung over them.
entries.2:7: They asked again for the dream to be told to them, promising to explain it. They had no idea yet how impossible the king's demand really was.
entries.2:8: The king accused them of stalling for time because they knew they could not do it. He did not trust them and assumed they were trying to trick him.
entries.2:9: He said their only hope was to tell him the dream, and he suspected they were making up lies to buy time. He was determined to test whether they truly had any real power.
entries.2:10: The experts admitted no one on earth could do what the king asked, and no king had ever demanded such a thing. They were admitting their limits and the unreasonableness of the request.
entries.2:11: They said only the gods could reveal such a thing, and those gods do not live among people. They were saying the answer was beyond any human being.
entries.2:12: The king flew into a rage and ordered all the wise men of Babylon to be killed. A proud ruler's anger can turn deadly for everyone around him.
entries.2:13: The order went out to execute the wise men, and they came looking for Daniel and his friends too. Innocent people were about to die because of one man's fury.
entries.2:14: Daniel spoke carefully and sensibly to the captain of the guard who was carrying out the executions. Staying calm and respectful in a crisis can open doors.
entries.2:15: Daniel asked the captain why the king's order was so harsh, and the captain explained what had happened. Asking questions calmly can help you understand a dangerous situation.
entries.2:16: Daniel went to the king and asked for time, promising to explain the dream. He stepped forward with courage and confidence when everyone else had given up.
entries.2:17: Daniel went home and told his three friends what was happening. He did not try to face the crisis alone but brought others into it.
entries.2:18: He asked them to pray for God's mercy about the secret, so they would not be killed with the other wise men. He knew their only real hope was God's help.
entries.2:19: That night God revealed the secret to Daniel in a vision, and Daniel praised God. God answered the prayer and Daniel responded with gratitude right away.
entries.2:20: Daniel praised God's name forever, saying wisdom and strength belong to him. He gave God the credit before explaining anything else.
entries.2:21: God controls the rise and fall of kings and gives wisdom and knowledge to people. History is not random; God is at work behind the scenes.
entries.2:22: God reveals deep secrets and knows what is hidden in darkness, and light dwells with him. Nothing is too hidden for God to see or too mysterious for him to reveal.
entries.2:23: Daniel thanked God for giving him wisdom and strength and for revealing what they had asked. He acknowledged that the answer came from God, not himself.
entries.2:24: Daniel went to the captain and asked him not to kill the wise men, saying he would explain the dream to the king. He used his answer from God to save others, not just himself.
entries.2:25: The captain quickly brought Daniel before the king, introducing him as a captive from Judah. Daniel's chance came through an unlikely door, but God had arranged it.
entries.2:26: The king asked Daniel, also called Belteshazzar, whether he could tell him the dream and its meaning. The king was testing whether this young captive could really do it.
entries.2:27: Daniel told the king that no wise man or magician could explain the secret he was asking about. He was honest that human experts had no answer.
entries.2:28: Daniel said there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has shown the king what will happen in the last days. Daniel pointed straight to God as the source.
entries.2:29: Daniel told the king that his nighttime thoughts were about what would happen in the future, and God had revealed it to him. God was answering the king's own anxious wondering.
entries.2:30: Daniel said the secret was revealed not because he was wiser than anyone else, but so the king could know the meaning and understand his own thoughts. Daniel stayed humble and kept the focus on the king's need.
entries.2:31: Daniel described a huge, dazzling statue that stood before the king and frightened him. The dream was vivid and its appearance alone was terrifying.
entries.2:32: The statue's head was gold, its chest and arms silver, and its belly and thighs bronze. Each part was made of a different, less valuable metal.
entries.2:33: Its legs were iron, and its feet were partly iron and partly clay. The statue was a mix of strong and weak materials.
entries.2:34: As the king watched, a stone was cut out without hands and struck the statue's feet of iron and clay, breaking them. Something not made by human hands brought the whole thing down.
entries.2:35: The iron, clay, bronze, silver, and gold were all crushed together and blown away like chaff, and the stone grew into a mountain filling the whole earth. What looked permanent was swept away, while the stone kept growing.
entries.2:36: Daniel said this was the dream, and now he would explain its meaning to the king. He moved from describing the dream to interpreting it.
entries.2:37: Daniel told the king that the God of heaven had given him his kingdom, power, strength, and glory. Even a pagan king's authority came from God.
entries.2:38: God had put all people, animals, and birds under the king's rule, and Daniel said the king was the head of gold. The king's greatness was real, but it was given to him by God.
entries.2:39: After the king would come another kingdom lower than his, then a third kingdom of bronze that would rule over all the earth. The statue's metals pointed to a series of kingdoms that would follow one another.
entries.2:40: A fourth kingdom would be strong as iron, crushing and smashing everything like iron does. This kingdom would be powerful and destructive, breaking down all that came before it.
entries.2:41: The kingdom shown in the dream is divided, with some parts strong like iron and others weak like clay. It means a powerful nation will be split and not hold together evenly.
entries.2:42: The mix of iron and clay in the toes shows that this kingdom will be partly strong and partly fragile. Some of it will stand firm while other parts break easily.
entries.2:43: The rulers will try to join themselves together through marriage, but the union will not hold, just as iron and clay do not truly mix. Human alliances cannot make a divided kingdom solid.
entries.2:44: God himself will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed and will outlast every human empire. It will replace all earthly kingdoms and last forever, which gives the reader lasting hope.
entries.2:45: The stone cut without hands shows that this kingdom comes from God, not from human effort, and it will crush all other powers. God has revealed the future to the king, and the dream is certain to happen.
entries.2:46: The king was so overwhelmed that he bowed before Daniel and ordered gifts and incense for him. It shows how deeply the explanation of the dream affected him.
entries.2:47: The king openly declared that Daniel's God is above all gods and reveals hidden things. A pagan ruler came to acknowledge the true God's power through Daniel.
entries.2:48: The king rewarded Daniel with many gifts and put him in charge of Babylon and its wise men. God honored Daniel's faithfulness with great responsibility and status.
entries.2:49: Daniel asked that his three friends be given authority over the province's affairs, while he stayed close to the king. Daniel used his position to help others and kept his place of influence.
entries.3:1: The king set up a huge gold statue on a plain in Babylon, probably to honor himself or his gods. It shows how easily a powerful leader can demand attention and loyalty that belongs to God alone.
entries.3:2: The king summoned all his officials to come to the dedication of the statue. He wanted the whole government to witness and take part in this public display of loyalty.
entries.3:3: The officials all came and stood in front of the statue as ordered. Crowds and leaders can be swept along into doing what is wrong when everyone else is doing it.
entries.3:4: A herald shouted a command to everyone of every people and language. The demand was meant to be heard by all, so no one could claim they didn't know.
entries.3:5: At the sound of the music, everyone was ordered to bow down and worship the gold statue. Music and ceremony were being used to pressure people into worshiping something other than God.
entries.3:6: Anyone who refused to bow would be thrown into a blazing furnace that very hour. The penalty was severe, so bowing was a matter of life and death.
entries.3:7: When the music played, all the people bowed down to the statue as commanded. Most people went along with the crowd, showing how strong the pressure to conform can be.
entries.3:8: Some Chaldeans came forward and accused the Jews to the king. They used the situation to turn the king against God's people.
entries.3:9: They addressed the king with a respectful wish for his long life. This was a polite way to begin their accusation against the Jews.
entries.3:10: They reminded the king of his own command about bowing when the music played. They were setting up their case by restating the rule he had made.
entries.3:11: They also repeated the punishment for refusing to bow. They wanted the king to feel his authority was being challenged.
entries.3:12: They named Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego as Jews the king had put in charge, saying these men ignored his command and would not worship his gods or the statue. Their faithfulness to God made them a target.
entries.3:13: The king became furious and ordered the three men brought to him. His anger shows how personally he took their refusal to obey.
entries.3:14: The king asked them directly whether it was true they would not serve his god or bow to the statue. He gave them a chance to explain or change their minds.
entries.3:15: The king offered them one more chance to bow, warning that otherwise they would be burned, and he mocked them by asking what god could rescue them from his power. He was daring God to prove himself.
entries.3:16: The three men answered the king calmly, saying they didn't need to argue their case. They were not going to debate or negotiate about their loyalty to God.
entries.3:17: They said that if their God was able, he would rescue them from the fire and from the king's power. They trusted God's ability even while leaving the outcome to him.
entries.3:18: They added that even if God did not rescue them, they still would not serve the king's gods or bow to the statue. Their commitment to God did not depend on getting a miracle.
entries.3:19: The king's face twisted with rage, and he ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. His fury grew because the men would not back down.
entries.3:20: He ordered strong soldiers to tie the three men up and throw them into the blazing furnace. The king used his full force against them.
entries.3:21: The men were thrown into the fire still wearing their coats, trousers, hats, and other clothes, tied with ropes. They had no chance to prepare or escape.
entries.3:22: The furnace was so fiercely hot that the soldiers who threw the three men in were killed by the flames. The king's own order turned against his own men.
entries.3:23: The three men, still tied, fell down into the blazing fire. From a human point of view, it looked like the end for them.
entries.3:24: The king jumped up in alarm and asked his advisors whether three men had been thrown in, and they confirmed it. Something unexpected was happening inside the fire.
entries.3:25: The king saw four men walking around loose in the fire, unharmed, and the fourth looked like a divine being. God had not abandoned them; he was with them in the flames.
entries.3:26: The king called the three men out of the fire as servants of the Most High God, and they came out. Even a pagan king had to acknowledge God's power.
entries.3:27: The officials crowded around and saw that the fire had not harmed the men at all—not a hair was singed, their clothes were fine, and they didn't even smell of smoke. God's rescue was complete and undeniable.
entries.3:28: The king praised the God of the three men, saying God had sent his angel to save those who trusted him and who defied the king's command rather than worship any other god. Their courage led even the king to honor God.
entries.3:29: The king made a decree that anyone who spoke evil against their God would be destroyed, because no other god could save like this. God's power had changed the king's policy, at least for now.
entries.3:30: The king gave the three men even greater authority in Babylon. God honored their faithfulness, and their stand for him led to promotion rather than ruin.
entries.4:1: The king is writing to people everywhere and wishing them peace. It shows that even a pagan king wanted good things for everyone under his rule.
entries.4:2: Nebuchadnezzar wants to tell everyone about the amazing things God did for him. When God does something big in your life, it's worth sharing with others.
entries.4:3: He praises God's miracles and says God's rule never ends. Whatever powerful rulers come and go, God is still in charge forever.
entries.4:4: The king was comfortable and successful, with everything going well at home. It's easy to feel secure when life is easy, but that can make us forget God.
entries.4:5: A dream terrified him and left him shaken. Even powerful people can be frightened by things they can't control or understand.
entries.4:6: He called in all his experts to explain the dream. When we're confused or afraid, we often look for someone who can help us understand.
entries.4:7: His usual advisors and fortune-tellers couldn't explain the dream. Human wisdom and magic have limits; not every problem can be solved by experts.
entries.4:8: Finally Daniel came, a man known to have God's spirit in him. God often uses faithful people to bring clarity when others fail.
entries.4:9: The king trusts Daniel because he believes God's spirit is with him. Being known as someone close to God gives you credibility with others.
entries.4:10: He describes seeing a huge tree in the middle of the earth. The dream's image is simple but its meaning will turn out to be about something much bigger.
entries.4:11: The tree grew enormous, reaching to the sky and visible everywhere. It pictures something or someone whose influence spreads across the whole world.
entries.4:12: The tree provided food and shelter for animals and birds. A good ruler or powerful person can be a blessing that supports many others.
entries.4:13: He saw a holy messenger coming down from heaven. God sends his messengers to deliver messages, even to kings who don't know him.
entries.4:14: The messenger orders the tree cut down and its branches stripped. This is a picture of sudden judgment that removes what seemed permanent.
entries.4:15: The stump and roots are left in the ground, bound with iron and brass. Judgment is real, but it's not the end—there's still a root left for restoration.
entries.4:16: The person will lose his human mind and live like an animal for seven periods of time. Pride can bring a person lower than they ever imagined.
entries.4:17: The heavenly watchers decree this so everyone will know the Most High rules over human kingdoms. God is the one who raises up and brings down rulers, often using the least likely people.
entries.4:18: The king asks Daniel to interpret because his other wise men couldn't. He recognizes that Daniel has something the others don't—God's spirit.
entries.4:19: Daniel is troubled and hesitant to give the bad news. The king kindly tells him not to worry, and Daniel wishes the judgment were on the king's enemies instead. A faithful messenger speaks hard truth with compassion.
entries.4:20: Daniel repeats the image of the great tree to make sure the king understands. Good teaching restates the picture before explaining its meaning.
entries.4:21: He recalls how the tree gave shade and food to the animals and birds. The details matter because they show how much the king's greatness benefited others.
entries.4:22: The tree is Nebuchadnezzar himself—his power and rule have grown to reach the whole earth. The dream is personal, and it's about him.
entries.4:23: He reminds the king of the watcher's command to cut down the tree but leave the stump. The dream has both a warning and a hidden promise of hope.
entries.4:24: Daniel says this is God's decision against the king. The dream isn't random—it's a direct message from the Most High to a specific person.
entries.4:25: The king will be driven out to live like an animal until he acknowledges God's rule. Pride will be broken, and the lesson will last until he learns who is really in charge.
entries.4:26: The stump left in the ground means the kingdom will be restored once the king recognizes heaven's authority. Even in judgment, God leaves room for restoration.
entries.4:27: Daniel urges the king to stop sinning, do right, and show mercy to the poor, which may delay the judgment. Turning from sin and caring for the needy is the right response to a warning.
entries.4:28: Everything Daniel predicted happened to the king. God's warnings are not empty threats—what he says comes true.
entries.4:29: A full year passed before judgment came. God gives people time to change, but the delay doesn't mean the warning was false.
entries.4:30: The king boasted that he had built Babylon by his own power and for his own glory. Pride takes credit for what God has allowed us to accomplish.
entries.4:31: While he was still boasting, a voice from heaven declared his kingdom taken away. Pride can be cut down in an instant, even mid-sentence.
entries.4:32: He will live like an animal until he admits the Most High rules over human kingdoms. The lesson is designed to teach him who really holds power.
entries.4:33: The judgment happened immediately—he lived like an ox, with hair and nails growing wild. The proud king was humbled in the most humiliating way imaginable.
entries.4:34: When he looked up to heaven, his sanity returned, and he praised God. Recognizing God's authority is the turning point that restores a person.
entries.4:35: All people are nothing compared to God, and no one can stop him or question what he does. God is completely sovereign, and we are not.
entries.4:36: His sanity, honor, and kingdom were restored, and he became even stronger than before. God doesn't just judge—he restores those who humble themselves.
entries.4:37: The king now praises God, saying his works are true and he humbles the proud. The lesson of the whole chapter is that pride brings you down, but God is faithful and just.
entries.5:1: Belshazzar, the king, threw a huge party for a thousand of his important guests and drank wine in front of them all. It shows a leader more focused on showing off and having a good time than on caring for his kingdom.
entries.5:2: While drunk, Belshazzar ordered the sacred gold and silver cups taken from God's temple in Jerusalem to be brought out for his guests to drink from. He was treating holy things as party toys, which was a deliberate insult to God.
entries.5:3: So the temple cups were brought in, and the king, his nobles, and the women with them all drank wine from them. They were using what belonged to God for their own pleasure.
entries.5:4: As they drank, they praised gods made of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone. They gave credit to lifeless idols instead of the real God.
entries.5:5: Right then, fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster wall of the king's palace, and the king saw the hand as it wrote. Something supernatural interrupted their party.
entries.5:6: The king turned pale, his thoughts terrified him, his strength drained away, and his knees knocked together. Even a powerful king can be reduced to fear in a moment.
entries.5:7: The king shouted for his enchanters, astrologers, and fortune-tellers and promised that whoever could read and explain the writing would get a purple robe, a gold chain, and high rank in the kingdom. He was desperate and trying to buy an answer.
entries.5:8: All the king's wise men came in, but none of them could read the writing or explain what it meant. Human wisdom and magic had no answer for what God had written.
entries.5:9: This made King Belshazzar even more terrified and pale, and his nobles were completely confused too. The whole party turned into panic.
entries.5:10: The queen came into the banquet hall and told the king to calm down and not be so frightened. She stepped in to steady a king who had lost his nerve.
entries.5:11: She reminded him that there was a man in the kingdom who had the spirit of the holy gods and whose insight and wisdom had been proven in his father's time, and that Nebuchadnezzar had put him in charge of all the wise men. She pointed him toward the one person who might actually help.
entries.5:12: She explained that this man, Daniel (also called Belteshazzar), had an extraordinary spirit and could interpret dreams, explain riddles, and solve hard problems, so the king should send for him. She was recommending Daniel because of his real track record.
entries.5:13: Daniel was brought before the king, who asked him if he was the Daniel brought from Judah as a captive by the king's father. The king was meeting the man he had heard about.
entries.5:14: The king told Daniel he had heard that the spirit of the gods was in him and that he had insight, understanding, and unusual wisdom. He was flattering Daniel before asking for help.
entries.5:15: The king admitted that his wise men and enchanters had been brought in to read the writing and explain it, but they couldn't. He was acknowledging that his own experts had failed.
entries.5:16: The king told Daniel that he had heard Daniel could explain things and solve hard questions, and he repeated the reward of a purple robe, a gold chain, and high rank if Daniel could read and explain the writing. He was still trying to bargain with a reward.
entries.5:17: Daniel told the king to keep his gifts and give his rewards to someone else, but he would still read the writing and explain it to him. Daniel wasn't in it for the money; he was going to tell the truth regardless.
entries.5:18: Daniel began by reminding the king that the Most High God had given his father Nebuchadnezzar the kingdom, great power, glory, and honor. He was setting up the story to show who really gives and takes power.
entries.5:19: Because of the great power God gave him, all peoples and nations feared Nebuchadnezzar, and he could kill or spare, raise up or bring down, whoever he wanted. His authority was enormous, but it had been given to him.
entries.5:20: But when Nebuchadnezzar became proud and hard-hearted, he was removed from his throne and stripped of his glory. Pride was the turning point that brought him down.
entries.5:21: He was driven away from people, lived like an animal eating grass, and was soaked with dew until he finally acknowledged that the Most High God rules over human kingdoms and gives power to whomever he chooses. It took a humbling experience for him to learn who is really in charge.
entries.5:22: Daniel told Belshazzar that even though he knew all this about his father, he had not humbled himself but remained proud. Knowing the lesson didn't help because he refused to apply it.
entries.5:23: Belshazzar had set himself against the Lord of heaven by drinking from his temple cups and praising gods of silver, gold, bronze, iron, wood, and stone that can't see, hear, or know anything, while ignoring the God who holds his very breath and all his ways. He honored powerless idols and dishonored the God who gave him life.
entries.5:24: That is why the hand was sent from God and the writing was inscribed on the wall. The writing was a direct response to Belshazzar's arrogance against God.
entries.5:25: The writing on the wall was: Mene, Tekel, Peres. These were the words God had written.
entries.5:26: Mene means that God has counted the days of Belshazzar's kingdom and brought it to an end. His time as king was up.
entries.5:27: Tekel means that Belshazzar was weighed on God's scales and found to be lacking. God had measured him and he came up short.
entries.5:28: Peres means that Belshazzar's kingdom was divided and given to the Medes and Persians. His kingdom was being handed over to others.
entries.5:29: Belshazzar gave the order, and Daniel was dressed in purple, given a gold chain, and publicly declared to be a high official in the kingdom. The king kept his promise, even though the news was bad.
entries.5:30: That same night, Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was killed. The judgment God announced happened immediately.
entries.5:31: Darius the Mede then took over the kingdom at about sixty-two years old. A new ruler took the throne the same night the old one fell.
entries.6:1: Darius organized his empire by appointing 120 officials to govern throughout the land. This shows that good leadership involves structure and shared responsibility.
entries.6:2: Three supervisors, including Daniel, oversaw those officials so the king wouldn't lose money or be cheated. Honest oversight protects everyone involved.
entries.6:3: Daniel did his job so well, because of a special spirit within him, that the king planned to promote him over the whole kingdom. Doing excellent work can bring unexpected opportunities.
entries.6:4: His rivals tried hard to find fault with Daniel's work but found nothing wrong, because he was honest and faithful. A life of integrity leaves enemies with nothing to accuse you of.
entries.6:5: The rivals realized the only way to trap Daniel was through his faith in God. Sometimes people attack what matters most to you when they can't find anything else.
entries.6:6: The officials came to the king with flattering words, wishing him long life. Flattery is often a tool people use to get what they want.
entries.6:7: They claimed everyone agreed on a law that for thirty days no one could pray to anyone except the king, and violators would be thrown to the lions. A united front can be deceptive, and pressure to go along with the crowd is dangerous.
entries.6:8: They urged the king to sign the decree so it couldn't be changed, like all Medo-Persian laws. Leaders should be careful about signing things they can't undo.
entries.6:9: Darius signed the written order without realizing the trap. Decisions made quickly or under pressure can have serious consequences.
entries.6:10: When Daniel heard about the law, he went home and prayed on his knees three times a day, just as he always had. Faithful habits built over a lifetime give strength when trouble comes.
entries.6:11: The men spied on Daniel and caught him praying and asking God for help. People who want to harm you will watch for any opportunity.
entries.6:12: They reminded the king of his own decree, and he confirmed it couldn't be changed. Be careful what you commit to, because some promises can't be taken back.
entries.6:13: They accused Daniel of ignoring the king and his order by praying three times a day. They twisted his faithfulness to God into an act of rebellion.
entries.6:14: The king was very upset and spent the whole day trying to find a way to save Daniel. Even those in power can be trapped by their own decisions.
entries.6:15: The men insisted that no law the king made could be changed. Pressure from others can push a leader into doing something he doesn't want to do.
entries.6:16: The king gave the order and Daniel was thrown into the lions' pit, with the king saying Daniel's God would protect him. Even in a hopeless situation, words of faith can bring comfort.
entries.6:17: A stone was placed over the pit and sealed with the king's and the lords' stamps so nothing could be altered. Human efforts to secure a situation can't stop God's plans.
entries.6:18: The king went home but couldn't eat or sleep all night, worrying about Daniel. A guilty conscience can rob anyone of peace.
entries.6:19: At dawn the king hurried to the lions' pit. Genuine concern makes people act quickly and personally.
entries.6:20: The king called out in anguish, asking whether Daniel's God could save him. Even a pagan king was moved to ask about the power of the living God.
entries.6:21: Daniel answered the king calmly, wishing him long life. A peaceful response in a crisis shows real trust in God.
entries.6:22: Daniel explained that God sent an angel to shut the lions' mouths because he was innocent before God and the king. God can protect those who stay faithful and honest.
entries.6:23: The king was overjoyed and had Daniel lifted out unharmed because he trusted in God. Faith in God is what carried Daniel through.
entries.6:24: The men who accused Daniel were thrown into the pit with their families and were killed before reaching the bottom. Those who plot evil often fall into their own trap.
entries.6:25: Darius wrote to all the peoples and languages in his empire, wishing them peace. A dramatic event can move even a king to speak to everyone.
entries.6:26: The king ordered everyone in his kingdom to fear Daniel's God, the living God whose kingdom will never end. God's power can turn a pagan ruler into a witness for him.
entries.6:27: Darius praised God as the one who saves, rescues, and performs signs and wonders, and who kept Daniel safe from the lions. God's rescue of one person can become a testimony to many.
entries.6:28: Daniel prospered throughout the reigns of Darius and Cyrus the Persian. Faithfulness to God can lead to lasting success, even in a foreign land.
entries.7:1: Daniel had a dream from God and wrote it down so others could know what he saw. It reminds us that God gives people understanding and wants it remembered.
entries.7:2: In his dream Daniel saw strong winds stirring up a huge sea. The sea stands for the nations of the world in turmoil.
entries.7:3: Four huge beasts came up out of the sea, each one different from the others. These beasts stand for powerful kingdoms that would rise in the world.
entries.7:4: The first beast looked like a lion with eagle's wings, but its wings were torn off and it was made to stand and think like a man. This pictures a proud empire being humbled and changed.
entries.7:5: The second beast looked like a bear raised up on one side, with ribs in its mouth, and it was told to eat much meat. This pictures a fierce kingdom that conquers and devours others.
entries.7:6: The third beast looked like a leopard with four wings and four heads, and it was given ruling power. This pictures a fast-moving kingdom that spreads quickly and rules widely.
entries.7:7: The fourth beast was terrifying and very strong, with iron teeth, and it crushed everything underfoot; it had ten horns. This pictures a harsh kingdom more fearsome than all the others.
entries.7:8: While Daniel watched, a small horn grew up and uprooted three of the other horns, and it had human eyes and a mouth that boasted. This pictures a proud ruler who rises by pushing others aside.
entries.7:9: Then Daniel saw thrones set in place and God, pictured as an ancient figure, take his seat with fire around him. This shows God is the eternal judge who rules over all.
entries.7:10: A river of fire flowed from God's presence, and countless thousands served him as the court sat and the books were opened. This means God sees everything and will judge fairly.
entries.7:11: Because of the boastful words of the little horn, Daniel watched until the fourth beast was killed and burned up. This shows that arrogant evil will finally be destroyed.
entries.7:12: The other beasts lost their authority, though they were allowed to live a little longer. This means no earthly power lasts forever; God sets the limits.
entries.7:13: Daniel saw someone like a human figure coming with the clouds of heaven, and he was brought before God. This points to a ruler chosen by God himself.
entries.7:14: This figure was given everlasting authority, glory, and a kingdom that all peoples would serve and that would never end. This means God's chosen king will rule forever and cannot be overthrown.
entries.7:15: Daniel was deeply troubled and disturbed by what he had seen in the vision. It is normal for even faithful people to feel shaken by frightening things.
entries.7:16: Daniel asked one of those standing nearby what the vision meant, and he was promised an explanation. God is willing to help us understand what confuses us.
entries.7:17: The four great beasts stand for four kings who will rise on the earth. The vision is about real rulers and kingdoms in history.
entries.7:18: But God's holy people will receive the kingdom and keep it forever and ever. However bad things get, God's people have a lasting hope.
entries.7:19: Daniel wanted to know more about the fourth beast, which was so different and terrifying, with iron teeth and bronze claws that crushed everything. He wanted to understand the worst of what he had seen.
entries.7:20: He also wanted to understand the ten horns and the little horn that rose up and caused three to fall, the one with eyes and a boastful mouth that seemed greater than the rest. He was asking about the proud ruler who would stand out.
entries.7:21: Daniel saw that this horn made war on God's holy people and defeated them for a time. God's people can face real suffering and seeming defeat.
entries.7:22: But then God, the ancient judge, came, and the decision was made to give authority to his holy people, and the time came for them to receive the kingdom. God's justice comes in his own time.
entries.7:23: The fourth beast stands for a fourth kingdom, different from the others, that will crush and smash the whole earth. This is a warning about a harsh and overwhelming power.
entries.7:24: The ten horns are ten kings from that kingdom, and after them another king will rise who is different and will bring down three kings. Power often shifts, and proud rulers replace one another.
entries.7:25: This king will speak against God, try to wear down his holy people, and try to change times and laws, and God's people will be under his power for a set period. God's people may suffer, but the time is limited by God.
entries.7:26: But the court will sit in judgment, and this king's authority will be ended and completely destroyed. No matter how powerful evil seems, God will bring it to an end.
entries.7:27: The kingdom, authority, and power over all the earth will be given to God's holy people, and his kingdom will last forever with all powers serving him. God's people will finally share in his lasting rule.
entries.7:28: That was the end of the vision, and Daniel was deeply troubled, his face turned pale, but he kept it to himself. Even hard truths from God can weigh heavily on us, and sometimes we must hold them quietly.
entries.8:1: Daniel has another vision about two years after the first one, while Belshazzar is still king. It reminds the reader that God keeps speaking to his people over time.
entries.8:2: In the vision Daniel finds himself near a canal by the city of Susa in Elam. The setting matters because it becomes the stage for what he is about to see.
entries.8:3: He sees a ram with two horns, one longer than the other and growing later. The picture is of a powerful kingdom that rises in stages.
entries.8:4: The ram pushes in every direction and nothing can stop it, so it becomes proud and does as it pleases. Power that no one can check easily turns into arrogance.
entries.8:5: A goat comes charging from the west so fast it seems not to touch the ground, with one big horn between its eyes. This introduces a swift, aggressive new power.
entries.8:6: The goat rushes furiously at the two-horned ram. The vision shows one empire violently replacing another.
entries.8:7: The goat knocks the ram down and smashes its horns, and no one can rescue the ram. The stronger power wins completely, which is how human kingdoms often treat each other.
entries.8:8: The goat becomes very strong, but then its great horn breaks and four horns grow in its place toward the four directions. A sudden change of leadership splits the empire into parts.
entries.8:9: From one of those horns a small horn grows and becomes very great, reaching toward the south, the east, and the beautiful land. A minor-looking power grows into a major threat, especially to God's land.
entries.8:10: It grows so proud that it even attacks the army of heaven and throws some of the stars to the ground. This pictures a ruler who sets himself against God's people and God's order.
entries.8:11: It exalts itself against the commander of the army, stops the regular offering, and ruins the sanctuary. The heart of the offense is that it attacks worship of God himself.
entries.8:12: Because of rebellion, the regular offering is handed over and truth is thrown down, and the horn succeeds in what it does. Wrong seems to win for a time, which is deeply troubling to faithful people.
entries.8:13: Daniel hears holy beings ask how long the offering will be stopped and the sanctuary trampled. It is a real question believers ask when evil seems to go on and on.
entries.8:14: The answer is 2,300 evenings and mornings, after which the sanctuary will be restored. The point is that the suffering has a limit and God sets the time for cleansing and recovery.
entries.8:15: Daniel wants to understand the vision, and then a figure in human form appears before him. God responds to the honest desire to understand what he is doing.
entries.8:16: A voice calls out to Gabriel to explain the vision to Daniel. God provides an interpreter so his servant is not left confused.
entries.8:17: Gabriel comes near, Daniel falls down in fear, and Gabriel tells him the vision concerns the time of the end. The message is serious because it points to a final period of history.
entries.8:18: While Gabriel speaks, Daniel falls into a deep sleep, but Gabriel touches him and sets him back on his feet. God gently strengthens his servant so he can receive the message.
entries.8:19: Gabriel explains that the vision concerns the later time of wrath, at an appointed time. The events are not random; they fit God's fixed timetable.
entries.8:20: The two-horned ram stands for the kings of Media and Persia. The symbols are explained plainly so Daniel knows which powers are meant.
entries.8:21: The goat stands for the king of Greece, and the big horn is its first king. The vision is predicting the rise of Greece and its famous leader.
entries.8:22: The broken horn means that after the first king, four kingdoms will rise from his nation, but none will match his power. Empires fragment after their strongest leader is gone.
entries.8:23: In the later part of those kingdoms, when evil has reached its full measure, a bold and crafty king will arise. Wickedness grows until God allows a decisive figure to appear.
entries.8:24: His power will be great, he will succeed in his schemes, and he will destroy the mighty and the holy people. Strength and success are not proof of God's approval.
entries.8:25: He will use deceit, destroy many who feel safe, and even defy the Prince of princes, but he will be broken without human hands. No matter how high he rises, God himself will bring him down.
entries.8:26: Gabriel says the vision of the evenings and mornings is true and should be kept secret because it concerns the distant future. Some truths are given long before they happen and are meant to be trusted patiently.
entries.8:27: Daniel is physically drained for days, then goes back to the king's work, still stunned because no one could explain the vision. Encountering God's revelation can leave a person shaken, yet faithful duty continues.
entries.9:1: This verse sets the time and place: Daniel is living under a new king, Darius the Mede, who now rules over Babylon. It reminds the reader that God's people can end up under foreign rulers, and that God is still at work in those times.
entries.9:2: Daniel read the prophet Jeremiah's writings and realized that the seventy years of Jerusalem's ruin were almost over. It shows that reading and trusting God's word can move a person to pray and act.
entries.9:3: Daniel turned to God in earnest prayer, asking for mercy and going without food, wearing rough cloth and sitting in dust as signs of sorrow. It shows that serious prayer can involve real humility and sacrifice.
entries.9:4: Daniel begins his prayer by praising God as great and faithful, who keeps his promises to those who love him and obey him. It reminds the reader to start prayer by remembering who God is.
entries.9:5: Daniel openly admits that he and his people have sinned, done wrong, and turned away from God's commands. It shows that honest prayer names sin plainly instead of making excuses.
entries.9:6: The people ignored the prophets God sent to warn their kings, leaders, ancestors, and everyone in the land. It reminds the reader to listen when God speaks through his messengers.
entries.9:7: God is in the right, but the people carry shame, scattered far and near because of their sin against him. It shows that sin brings real shame, and that admitting it is the first step toward healing.
entries.9:8: Daniel repeats that shame belongs to the people, including their kings, leaders, and ancestors, because they sinned against God. It shows that no one, not even leaders, is above admitting wrong.
entries.9:9: Even though the people rebelled, God is full of mercy and ready to forgive. It gives the reader hope that no sin is beyond God's willingness to pardon those who turn to him.
entries.9:10: The people failed to listen to God and did not walk in the laws he gave through the prophets. It reminds the reader that hearing God's voice means actually doing what he says.
entries.9:11: All Israel broke God's law, so the curses written in Moses' law came upon them as promised. It shows that God keeps his warnings as faithfully as his promises.
entries.9:12: God carried out the disaster he had warned about, bringing on Jerusalem trouble worse than anything else under heaven. It reminds the reader that God's warnings are real and should be taken seriously.
entries.9:13: The disaster came just as Moses' law said, yet the people still did not turn to God or seek his favor. It shows that trouble is meant to lead people back to God, not just to be endured.
entries.9:14: God watched over the disaster and brought it about, yet he remained right in everything he did, while the people refused to listen. It reminds the reader that God is fair even when his discipline is painful.
entries.9:15: Daniel recalls how God powerfully rescued his people from Egypt and made a great name for himself, yet the people still sinned. It shows that remembering God's past faithfulness can deepen honest confession.
entries.9:16: Daniel asks God, because of his own righteousness, to turn his anger away from Jerusalem, which had become a disgrace among the nations because of sin. It shows that God's character, not our goodness, is the basis for asking mercy.
entries.9:17: Daniel begs God to hear his prayer and let his face shine on the ruined sanctuary, asking for the sake of God's own servants. It reminds the reader to pray boldly for God's honor to be restored.
entries.9:18: Daniel asks God to open his eyes and see the ruined city that bears his name, pleading not on the basis of the people's goodness but God's great mercy. It shows that our only real ground for prayer is God's compassion.
entries.9:19: Daniel urgently asks God to hear, forgive, and act without delay, for the sake of his own name and the city and people called by it. It reminds the reader that God's reputation, not our merit, is the strongest reason to pray.
entries.9:20: While Daniel was still praying and confessing his own sins and his people's sins, asking mercy for God's holy mountain, something was about to happen. It shows that God listens while we are still speaking.
entries.9:21: While Daniel was still praying, the angel Gabriel, whom he had seen before, came to him at the time of the evening sacrifice. It reminds the reader that God answers prayer promptly, even before we finish.
entries.9:22: Gabriel came to teach Daniel and told him plainly that he had come to give him understanding. It shows that God cares about helping his people understand what is happening.
entries.9:23: Gabriel says that as soon as Daniel began praying, a message went out, and he came because Daniel was deeply loved; he tells Daniel to think carefully about the vision. It reminds the reader that God hears the very first word of prayer and values the one praying.
entries.9:24: A period of seventy weeks is set for the people and the holy city to finish dealing with sin, bring in lasting righteousness, confirm the prophetic vision, and consecrate a most holy place. It shows that God has a set plan and timeline for dealing with sin and restoring what is holy.
entries.9:25: From the command to rebuild Jerusalem until the coming of an anointed prince is seven weeks, and the city will be rebuilt over sixty-two more weeks, though in troubled times. It reminds the reader that God's plan unfolds on a schedule, even when the process is difficult.
entries.9:26: After those sixty-two weeks, the anointed one will be cut off and left with nothing, and the city and sanctuary will be destroyed by a coming prince, with war and ruin continuing to the end. It shows that God's plan includes real suffering and loss, yet it is still under his control.
entries.9:27: A ruler will make a firm agreement with many for one week, then stop the sacrifices halfway through and set up something abominable, until the decreed destruction falls on him. It reminds the reader that evil powers rise for a time but do not escape God's final judgment.
entries.10:1: Daniel received a message from God that was true but very hard to understand, and he came to grasp its meaning. It reminds the reader that God can reveal difficult things to those who seek understanding.
entries.10:2: Daniel spent three full weeks deeply mourning and grieving. This shows that seeking God's answers can involve real sorrow and patient waiting.
entries.10:3: During those weeks Daniel gave up enjoyable food, meat, wine, and even ordinary grooming. He set aside normal comforts to focus on prayer, showing that some spiritual seeking calls for sacrifice.
entries.10:4: Daniel was standing beside a large river on a particular day. The setting matters because this is where the vision that follows took place.
entries.10:5: Daniel looked up and saw a man dressed in fine linen with a belt of pure gold. The clothing signals that this was a glorious, heavenly messenger rather than an ordinary person.
entries.10:6: The messenger's appearance was dazzling, like glowing metal and flashing fire, and his voice was powerful like a crowd or army. This description shows a being of overwhelming glory and authority.
entries.10:7: Only Daniel saw the vision; the men with him saw nothing but were so terrified they ran and hid. It shows that God's revelation can be given to one person while others remain unaware.
entries.10:8: Left alone, Daniel lost all his strength and his face went pale. Encountering such glory leaves a person feeling utterly weak and undone.
entries.10:9: When Daniel heard the messenger's voice, he fell into a deep sleep with his face to the ground. The overwhelming experience left him helpless before God's messenger.
entries.10:10: A hand touched Daniel and gently raised him onto his knees and hands. God's messenger comes to strengthen and lift up the one who has fallen.
entries.10:11: The messenger called Daniel greatly loved and told him to stand and listen, and Daniel stood up trembling. It shows that God values and speaks to ordinary people, even when they feel afraid.
entries.10:12: The messenger told Daniel not to fear, because God had heard his prayers from the very first day he humbled himself and sought understanding. It reassures the reader that God listens from the start, even when the answer is delayed.
entries.10:13: A spiritual power over Persia opposed the messenger for twenty-one days until Michael, a chief angel, came to help. It shows that unseen spiritual conflict can delay answers to prayer.
entries.10:14: The messenger came to explain what will happen to Daniel's people in the future. God sometimes reveals the future so his people can be prepared and trust him.
entries.10:15: After hearing this, Daniel was speechless and kept his face to the ground. The weight of the message left him completely overwhelmed.
entries.10:16: One who looked like a human touched Daniel's lips so he could speak, and Daniel told him the vision had left him in pain and without strength. God's messengers help people respond even when they feel crushed.
entries.10:17: Daniel asked how he could possibly talk with such a glorious lord when he had no strength or breath left. It expresses honest human weakness before something far greater.
entries.10:18: The one who looked like a man touched Daniel again and gave him strength. God does not leave his servants helpless; he strengthens them to receive what he has to say.
entries.10:19: The messenger told Daniel not to fear, wished him peace, and urged him to be strong, and Daniel was strengthened and ready to listen. God's words of peace give courage to fearful people.
entries.10:20: The messenger explained that he was returning to fight against the spiritual power over Persia, and that the power over Greece would come afterward. It shows that history is played out amid unseen spiritual battles.
entries.10:21: The messenger said he would return to war against Persia and that Greece would follow, with only Michael standing with him. It reminds the reader that God's side may seem few, but his angels are at work in the affairs of nations.
entries.11:1: Daniel says that back when Darius the Mede first became king, he himself worked to support and strengthen him. It shows God's servants can be involved in helping rulers and governments succeed.
entries.11:2: God tells Daniel that three more kings will rule Persia, and a fourth will be very rich and will stir up his power against Greece. It means God knows ahead of time how nations and empires will rise and clash.
entries.11:3: A powerful king will appear who rules as he pleases with great strength. It reminds us that human rulers can seem unstoppable for a time.
entries.11:4: Once that king is at his peak, his kingdom will be shattered and split four ways, and it won't go to his family or carry his same power. It shows that even the mightiest empires fall apart.
entries.11:5: The king of the south will be strong, but one of his commanders will become even stronger and rule a large territory. It means power often shifts from one leader to another.
entries.11:6: After some years the two sides will make a deal sealed by a marriage, but it won't hold and the woman and her supporters will be destroyed. It shows that alliances built on convenience often collapse.
entries.11:7: A member of her family line will rise up, attack the northern king's army and fortress, and defeat them. It means family ties and revenge can drive the next round of conflict.
entries.11:8: He will carry off the northern king's idols, images and valuable silver and gold to the south, and stay away from him for some years. It shows that even religious objects were treated as war loot.
entries.11:9: The northern king will invade the south but then retreat back to his own land. It means not every attack succeeds, and some campaigns end in withdrawal.
entries.11:10: The northern king's sons will gather a huge army, sweep through like a flood, and push the war right up to the southern king's fortress. It shows how conflict escalates from one generation to the next.
entries.11:11: The southern king will get angry, march out and fight, and though the northern king has a big army, it will be handed over to the south. It means anger can fuel a battle, and numbers don't guarantee victory.
entries.11:12: When the army is carried off, the southern king will become proud and cause the deaths of tens of thousands, but he won't become truly strong. It warns that success can go to your head and still leave you weak.
entries.11:13: The northern king will raise an even bigger army than before and attack again after some years with great wealth. It shows that defeated powers often come back stronger.
entries.11:14: In those days many will rise against the southern king, and violent men among Daniel's own people will try to force the vision to come true, but they will fail. It means trying to hurry God's plan by force ends badly.
entries.11:15: The northern king will come, build siege works and capture a fortified city, and the south's best troops won't be able to hold their ground. It shows that superior siege tactics can break even strong defenses.
entries.11:16: The invader will do as he pleases with no one able to stop him, and he will set himself up in the beautiful land with destruction in his hand. It means the land of Israel will fall under his control.
entries.11:17: He will plan to come with his full strength but instead make a treaty, offering a daughter in marriage to ruin the other side, yet his plan won't work. It shows that schemes wrapped in diplomacy can still fail.
entries.11:18: He will turn his attention to the coastlands and islands and capture many, but a commander will put an end to his insults and throw the shame back on him. It means bullying eventually meets resistance.
entries.11:19: He will turn back toward the strongholds of his own land, but he will be stopped, stumble and disappear from the scene. It shows that even a powerful ruler's end can come suddenly.
entries.11:20: His successor will send an official to collect taxes and enjoy royal splendor, but within a short time he will be destroyed, though not in anger or battle. It means some leaders fall quietly and unexpectedly.
entries.11:21: A despised nobody, who was never given royal honor, will take his place, coming in quietly and seizing the kingdom with smooth talk. It warns that flattery can be a weapon for taking power.
entries.11:22: His forces will be swept away and crushed before him, and even the leader of the covenant will meet the same fate. It means no alliance or treaty will protect people from him.
entries.11:23: Once people make an agreement with him, he will act deceitfully, and with only a small force he will suddenly rise up in arms. It shows that a treaty with a deceiver is no safety at all.
entries.11:24: He will invade rich regions and do what his ancestors never did, handing out plunder and property to gain followers, and he will plot against strongholds for a while. It means he buys loyalty with stolen wealth while planning his next move.
entries.11:25: He will throw his power and a large army against the southern king, and though the south fights with a very large and strong army, it will have to give way because of plots against him. It shows that betrayal from within can beat a bigger army.
entries.11:26: Those who eat his food will break him, his army will be wiped out, and many will fall by the sword. It means trusted insiders can cause a leader's collapse.
entries.11:27: Both kings will sit at one table with evil in their hearts, lying to each other, but it will accomplish nothing because the end will come at God's appointed time. It means deceitful deals between rulers don't change God's timetable.
entries.11:28: He will return home with great wealth, set his heart against the holy covenant, do as he pleases, and then go back to his own land. It shows that after a successful campaign he turns his hostility toward God's people.
entries.11:29: At the appointed time he will come back and invade the south again, but this time it won't go as it did before. It means past successes don't guarantee future victories.
entries.11:30: Ships from the west will come against him, and he will be afraid, turn back in rage against the holy covenant, and join forces with those who have abandoned it. It shows that fear and anger can turn a ruler against God's people and toward traitors.
entries.11:31: His soldiers will take their stand, desecrate the holy place and fortress, stop the regular offerings, and set up an abominable thing that causes horror. It means he will attack the very heart of worship.
entries.11:32: He will use smooth words to turn covenant-breakers toward sin, but those who know their God will stand firm and act. It means knowing God gives people strength to resist pressure and do what is right.
entries.11:33: The wise among the people will teach many others, but they will fall by sword and fire, be taken captive and robbed for a long time. It means faithful teachers often pay a high price.
entries.11:34: When they fall, they will get a little help, though many will join them insincerely. It means help in hard times can be small and mixed with people who aren't genuine.
entries.11:35: Some of the wise will stumble so they can be refined, purified and made clean until the time of the end, which is still set for a fixed time. It means even hard falls can serve God's purpose of purifying his people.
entries.11:36: The king will do as he pleases, exalt himself above every god, and speak shocking things against the God of gods, and he will succeed until the time of wrath is finished, because what is decreed will happen. It means arrogant rulers have a limit set by God.
entries.11:37: He will show no regard for the gods of his ancestors or the one desired by women, and no regard for any god at all, because he exalts himself above everything. It means his pride makes him reject every object of worship but himself.
entries.11:38: Instead he will honor a god of fortresses, a god his ancestors never knew, lavishing gold, silver, jewels and treasures on it. It means he will worship military power and wealth.
entries.11:39: He will use people who follow this foreign god to secure his strongest fortresses, give great honor to those he favors, make them rulers over many, and divide up land for a price. It means he rewards loyal followers with power and property.
entries.11:40: At the time of the end the southern king will attack him, and the northern king will come against him like a storm with chariots, horsemen and many ships, sweeping through many lands like a flood. It means the final conflict will be overwhelming and wide-reaching.
entries.11:41: A powerful king will invade the land of Israel and defeat many people, but a few neighboring nations will escape his control. It reminds the reader that even a mighty conqueror's reach has limits.
entries.11:42: He will extend his power over many countries, and the southern land will not escape him. No nation should assume it is safe from an aggressive ruler.
entries.11:43: He will seize the gold, silver, and treasures of the south, and people from Libya and Ethiopia will be forced to follow him. His success brings him wealth and power over others.
entries.11:44: Reports of trouble from the east and north will alarm him, and he will lash out in fierce anger to destroy many. Fear and rage drive him to greater violence.
entries.11:45: He will set up his royal camp between the sea and the holy mountain, but then he will fall with no one to help him. However powerful he becomes, his end comes suddenly and without support.
entries.12:1: An angel named Michael stands up to protect Daniel's people during a time of trouble worse than any before, and everyone whose name is written in God's book will be saved. It means God guards his people in the hardest times, so the reader can trust that being known by God matters most.
entries.12:2: People who have died will rise again, some to live forever and some to shame that never ends. It means death is not the end, and how we live now matters for what comes after.
entries.12:3: Those who are wise and who help others do right will shine brightly forever, like the sky and the stars. It means teaching and guiding people toward goodness is work with lasting honor.
entries.12:4: Daniel is told to seal up the book and keep it secret until the end time, when many will wander and trouble will increase. It means some things are not meant to be fully understood yet, and the reader should be patient rather than trying to force every detail.
entries.12:5: Daniel sees two other figures standing on opposite banks of the river. It sets the scene for the question that follows about how long these events will last.
entries.12:6: Daniel asks the man dressed in linen, who stands above the river, how long it will be until these amazing things are finished. It shows that even a faithful person wants to know when hard times will end.
entries.12:7: The man in linen raises both hands to heaven and swears by the God who lives forever that it will last a time, times, and half a time, and end when the holy people's suffering is complete. It means the hard period is set and limited by God, not endless.
entries.12:8: Daniel hears the answer but does not understand it, so he asks what it all means. It is honest to admit we don't grasp everything God is doing.
entries.12:9: Daniel is told to go on his way because the words are kept secret until the end time. It means not every answer is given now, and the reader should keep living faithfully without full understanding.
entries.12:10: Hard times will test and purify some people, while wrongdoers keep doing wrong and understand nothing, but the wise will see clearly. It means difficulty can refine a person, and understanding comes to those who seek it.
entries.12:11: Counting from when the daily sacrifice is stopped and a terrible thing is set up, there will be 1,290 days. It gives a specific, limited span, showing that the trouble has an end God has set.
entries.12:12: The person who waits and reaches 1,335 days is called blessed. It means patient endurance through the waiting is rewarded.
entries.12:13: Daniel is told to go his way, rest, and that he will rise to his place at the end of the days. It means he can live and die in peace, trusting God will raise him at the right time.
